title: Repairing a blown plaster bulge on a lath-and-plaster ceiling
subtitle: Remove detached plaster from a lath ceiling, re-tie loose laths, and replaster in two coats to restore a flat ceiling surface
excerpt: How to repair a blown plaster bulge on a lath-and-plaster ceiling. Covers testing for blown plaster, removing loose material safely, consolidating loose laths, applying a bonding scratch coat, and finishing with a multi-finish coat.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for heritage plasterwork repair.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pre-plasterboard ceiling and wall finish using thin strips of riven or sawn timber (laths) nailed horizontally across the joists at small gaps, with plaster applied in two or three coats. The first coat is pressed through the gaps to form keys that grip the plaster to the laths. Used in most domestic construction until the 1940s and 1950s.

The part of the first plaster coat that squeezes through the gaps between laths and spreads out on the back face of the ceiling to lock the plaster in place. When the key breaks, the plaster loses its grip on the ceiling and begins to sag or bulge.

The first plaster coat applied to laths or a masonry surface. It is pressed firmly into the surface, allowed to stiffen, and then scratched with a comb or nail to give a mechanical key for the finish coat above.

content.text: A blown plaster bulge is a patch where the plaster has lost its key on the laths above and detached from the ceiling. The repair removes the loose material, consolidates any broken laths, and replasters in two coats. INTERMEDIATE: consistent application technique is needed to get the finish coat level with the surrounding original plaster.
Test the ceiling and define the repair area

Tap the ceiling with a knuckle or the handle of a filling knife and listen for the hollow drum sound that indicates blown plaster. Work from the clear centre of the bulge outward until the tap returns a solid sound. Mark the boundary of the repair area. Clear the floor below and protect with dust sheets:
Pull away the blown plaster by hand or with the filling knife, working back to the solid boundary. Remove the

from the back of the laths with a scraper. Brush out all dust and debris from the lath gaps. Check each lath: split or loose laths should be secured with new screws into the joist above, or replaced with a short batten if badly split.
Wet the laths slightly before plastering so they do not draw moisture too quickly from the plaster. Mix bonding or browning plaster to a creamy consistency and trowel on the

firmly, pressing the plaster through the lath gaps to form keys. Build up to within 3 to 4 mm of the original plaster surface. When the coat begins to stiffen, scratch the surface with a comb or nail in a cross-hatch pattern. Allow to set hard, typically overnight.

Dampen the scratch coat. Mix multi-finish plaster to a smooth, lump-free paste. Apply a 2 to 3 mm coat over the repair area using the trowel in sweeping arcs, then flatten with the float in straight strokes. Feather the edges to blend into the surrounding ceiling. Polish with a slightly wet trowel as the plaster begins to stiffen. The finish coat is a thin working layer and sets quickly: mix only what you can use in 20 to 25 minutes.

attrs.symptom: Scratch coat pulls away from the laths when trowelled
attrs.cause: The laths were too dry and drew moisture out of the plaster before it could form keys.
attrs.fix: Dampen the laths with a brush or water spray before applying, and mix the plaster slightly stiffer to compensate.

attrs.symptom: Finish coat cracks in a map pattern as it dries
attrs.cause: The coat was too thick, or the scratch coat was not dampened before the finish coat was applied.
attrs.fix: Dampen the cracked finish, apply a thin slurry of finish plaster to fill the cracks, and trowel flat. Keep the next coat to 3 mm maximum.

attrs.symptom: Repair sags away from the ceiling before setting
attrs.cause: The plaster was mixed too wet, or too much material was applied in one coat.
attrs.fix: Allow the sagged material to harden, scrape back level, dampen, and apply a stiffer mix in thinner passes.
